source.title: The Curse of Helpfulness: Inverse Scaling Law in Robustness to Distractor Instructions via DistractionIF
source.authors: Zeli Su; Zhankai Xu; Tianlei Chen; Longfei Zheng; Xiaolu Zhang; Jun Zhou; Wentao Zhang

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong-document issue; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: It measures benchmark performance across model scales, a different measure and task from held-out pretraining loss, and reports an inverse trend relevant to downstream performance scaling.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or investigate compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its directly relevant result is a distraction-robustness benchmark score across model sizes. Output-path perplexities in the mechanistic analysis are not held-out pretraining loss. Paradigm-specific Figure 3 values are not available in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: It reports one downstream benchmark (DistractionIF pass rate) across Qwen3 sizes from 0.6B to 235B-A22B, and the score falls with scale. That result bears directly on V6's claim that downstream performance improves predictably with scale. It does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws or study allocation, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report inverse scaling of distraction robustness in non-thinking Qwen3 (65.97→37.6). They find thinking hurts small and mid dense models but helps MoE models. They attribute the decline to an eroding perplexity margin between gold and distracted outputs, and report that GRPO on Qwen3-8B improves robustness by up to 15.5 points without harming IFEval or IFBench.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a rubric-scored reference-text robustness benchmark and scale comparison, not held-out pretraining loss measurements, power-law fitting, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect varies with reasoning configuration and prompting paradigm; the text says non-thinking Qwen3 performance declines across all three paradigms, while thinking has different effects in smaller dense and larger MoE models.

fits_no_version.finding: Perplexity of fixed teacher (gold) responses falls with Qwen3 dense size (5.33 at 0.6B to 2.85 at 32B, with 1.7B higher at 5.98). Perplexity of distracted responses falls faster, so the margin ratio shrinks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perplexity on curated task outputs decreases with model size; this is not held-out pretraining loss.

record.problems: The text gives endpoint macro-average scores but no uncertainty estimates for them. Paradigm-specific scores are described as varying in Figure 3 but are not available in the supplied text. The authors note that the effects of MoE architecture and raw model scale cannot be decoupled because equivalent-sized dense baselines are lacking.
record.rows_left_out: Paradigm-specific Figure 3 scores were not extracted because their values are not present in the supplied text. Mechanistic output-path perplexities and GRPO pre/post results were left out because they do not measure downstream performance scaling with model size or held-out pretraining loss.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
No power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
No performance-vs-pretraining-loss relation. Only one task and one model family are scaled; no predictability fit.
No exponents or fitting choices examined.

missing.what: Single-turn DistractionIF scores for Qwen3 dense models 0.6B–32B, apparently about 57.8, 59.5, 53.1, 51.6, 46.1, 38.7. The figure-to-model mapping is inferred from extracted figure text. Note the 8B value (51.6) differs from Table 1's pre-RL 54.00.
Per-paradigm and thinking-mode scores across Qwen3 scales, and other model families.

record.verdict_notes: Scale is confounded with architecture (dense vs MoE) and with model-specific post-training; the authors acknowledge the MoE confound. The results are a single inverse-scaling benchmark judged by GPT-4o, with no error bars. The text's RMR for 0.6B (2.24) does not match the figure label (2.56). The perplexity analysis is not pretraining loss, so it does not bear on V1.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or large-run loss predictions.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token scaling fits.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count and loss.
The study evaluates a text robustness benchmark and a GRPO intervention, but does not test whether power-law loss scaling holds across modalities or training regimes.
Tests distraction-robustness benchmark performance across Qwen3 scale, not a broad set of downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, or analysis of how fitting choices affect scaling laws.

rows.subject: qwen3-0.6B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated distraction robustness as part of a Qwen3 model-scale comparison.

conditions.value: macro-average across single-turn, multi-turn, and system-prompt-driven

rows.note: The text reports this as the smaller-scale endpoint in the Qwen3 non-thinking comparison; this value alone does not establish the direction of change with scale.
rows.check: This is the small-scale endpoint (baseline) of the comparison. A single value cannot show a scale trend; it serves as R2's baseline.

rows.subject: qwen3-235B-a22b
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated distraction robustness as part of a Qwen3 model-scale comparison.

conditions.value: macro-average across single-turn, multi-turn, and system-prompt-driven

rows.note: The paper says the decline is visible across all three prompting paradigms, but gives these endpoint numbers as macro-averages.
rows.check: The score falls from 65.97 to 37.6 with scale. Caveats: the Qwen3 sizes differ in post-training and architecture (dense vs MoE), not only in scale, and no uncertainty is reported.

relationships.condition: Qwen3 family, non-thinking decoding, DistractionIF macro-average over three paradigms, 0.6B to 235B-A22B
relationships.reason: Pass rate falls from 65.97 to 37.6 as scale rises, an inverse trend (R1, R2). Figure 4's dense single-turn scores fall similarly from 1.7B to 32B (from the text; not yet in rows).
relationships.display_finding: Pass rate fell from 65.97 to 37.6 between 0.6B and 235B-A22B, while dense single-turn scores also declined from 1.7B to 32B.

relationships.condition: Qwen3 MoE models with thinking enabled
relationships.reason: Text only: authors say thinking gives gains and a 'phase transition to positive scaling' in MoE models. No numbers are given, so the inverse trend depends on decoding mode and architecture.
relationships.display_finding: Thinking improved performance and shifted MoE models toward positive scaling, making the size trend depend on decoding mode and architecture.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Qwen3 non-thinking comparison, 0.6B to 235B-A22B; macro-average across three interaction paradigms
reader_labels.reason: The reported macro-average pass rate falls from 65.97 to 37.6 as scale increases, contrary to downstream performance improving with scale in this tested setting (R1, R2).
